answer.summary: Base editors and prime editors both avoid the double-strand break that makes nuclease editing mutagenic, but trade off differently. Base editors (Komor 2016 for C-to-T, Gaudelli 2017 for A-to-G) are chemically simple, highly efficient and clinically far ahead, but make only transition mutations within a PAM-constrained window and cause bystander and guide-independent deamination; their flagship therapeutic use is knockout-by-splice-disruption (PCSK9, CAR7, HBG promoters) rather than precise repair. Prime editing (Anzalone 2019) is far more versatile - any substitution plus small indels, no bystander window - at the cost of lower efficiency and an oversized three-component payload that is much harder to deliver. That delivery asymmetry drives the evidence base: LNP-mRNA works well for base editors in liver and is re-dosable, so all peer-reviewed human in vivo results to date are base editing (VERVE-102 phase 1 in 35 patients, the VERVE-101 heart-1 report, and the bespoke N-of-1 CPS1 case), while base-edited ex vivo cell therapies (CAR7 T cells, BEAM-101) form the other clinical track. Prime editing has reached humans only ex vivo (PM359 for chronic granulomatous disease, n=2); its in vivo evidence remains entirely preclinical, progressing from dual-AAV (Boeck 2022, Davis 2023) through eVLP ribonucleoprotein delivery (An 2024) to the first credible LNP formulations in 2025-2026. Engineered virus-like particles occupy a middle ground: transient, DNA-free protein delivery that avoids both integrating transgenes and persistent expression, demonstrated first for base editors (Banskota 2022) and only later extended to prime editors and to cytosine editors. The 2025-2026 frontier is convergence - transient, non-viral, re-dosable prime-editor delivery and extension of both modalities beyond hepatocytes into CNS, retina and hematopoietic stem cells.

answer.summary:
Three DSB-free editing modalities form the backbone of this literature. Cytosine base editors (Komor 2016) and adenine base editors (Gaudelli 2017) chemically convert a base within a small window at a nicked locus: highly efficient (often >50-80%) but limited to transition mutations, with bystander-edit and deaminase-dependent off-target liabilities. Prime editing (Anzalone 2019) uses an nCas9-reverse transcriptase plus a pegRNA to write arbitrary substitutions and small indels, and with twinPE, kilobase-scale replacements; it is far more versatile but intrinsically less efficient and harder to deliver because it is a three-component system with a large cargo. The engineering arc is therefore about closing that gap: ABE8e for base editor speed; PE4/PE5/PEmax (mismatch-repair inhibition), epegRNAs and compact PE6 editors for prime editing.

Delivery cleanly separates the two. mRNA-LNP is transient, redosable and liver-tropic, and is the only route so far used for in vivo human editing (VERVE-102 for PCSK9; the bespoke CPS1 therapy for an infant). AAV gives durable expression but persistent editor exposure and a hard cargo limit, motivating size-optimized single-AAV ABEs and split/compact prime editors. Engineered virus-like particles deliver ribonucleoproteins transiently, combining viral tropism with the low off-target exposure of RNP delivery; they were demonstrated first for base editors (Banskota 2022) and then, with substantially more engineering, for prime editors (An 2024).

Evidence levels differ sharply by modality. Base editing has human clinical evidence in both compartments: ex vivo (base-edited CAR7 T cells 2023; risto-cel/BEAM-101 phase 1-2 for sickle cell, NEJM 2026) and in vivo (VERVE-102 phase 1, NEJM 2026; an n-of-1 CPS1 therapy, NEJM 2025). Prime editing has human clinical evidence only ex vivo (the PM359 CGD trial reported in NEJM in December 2025, which I could not verify bibliographically); all in vivo prime editing evidence remains preclinical - mouse liver, retina and brain, plus unpublished NHP data - though 2025-2026 LNP work now reports ~49% bulk mouse liver editing, which is the level at which clinical translation of in vivo prime editing becomes plausible.

answer.summary: Base editing (Komor 2016 for C>T, Gaudelli 2017 for A>G) and prime editing (Anzalone 2019) both avoid double-strand breaks, but differ in scope and maturity. Base editors are chemically simple, highly efficient, and limited to transition mutations (plus, with newer variants, some transversions); prime editors can install any substitution and small indels but are larger, slower, and more delivery-constrained. Engineering follow-ups split accordingly: ABE8e boosted base editor kinetics, while PEmax/PE4-PE5 (MMR suppression), epegRNAs, and compact PE6 reverse transcriptases were each needed to make prime editing practical. Delivery divides three ways. Ex vivo HSC/T-cell electroporation is the most clinically advanced route and has produced all four peer-reviewed human successes in cell therapy: base-edited CAR7 T cells (NEJM 2023), CS-101 for beta-thalassaemia (Nature 2026, five patients transfusion-independent at a median 23 months), and PM359 for p47phox CGD (NEJM 2025, the first prime editing in patients). In vivo LNP delivery to liver is next most mature, with a clean preclinical-to-clinical chain running from NHP PCSK9 editing (Musunuru 2021, Rothgangl 2021) to the YOLT-101 phase 1 (Nat Med 2026, 52% LDL-C reduction, no grade >=3 AEs) and the bespoke N-of-1 CPS1 treatment (NEJM 2025). Engineered VLPs sit at the preclinical frontier: they deliver editor ribonucleoprotein DNA-free, giving transient exposure and near-undetectable off-target editing (Banskota 2022), and have been extended to prime editor RNPs (An 2024), but no eVLP therapeutic has entered the clinic. AAV remains the workhorse for non-liver tissues (progeria, dual-AAV prime editing in brain/liver/heart) at the cost of prolonged editor expression. The sharpest distinction to preserve: every human result to date uses base editing except the single two-patient PM359 prime editing study, and all in vivo prime editing evidence - including the 2026 LNP formulation and the LNP/AAV hybrid - remains in mice.
gaps: DOIs for the pre-2024 entries (Komor, Gaudelli, Anzalone, Richter, Chen, Nelson, Doman, Koblan, Newby, Everette, Bock, Davis, Chiesa, Zuo) were supplied from domain knowledge rather than re-verified against the publisher in this session; spot-check before citing formally.

A 2026 Nature Biotechnology paper on VLP-delivered transformer base editors with uracil-DNA-glycosylase inhibition (Zhu/Ding/Liu, ShanghaiTech; ~46% Pcsk9 and ~64% Hpd liver editing) is directly on-topic for eVLP delivery but I could not retrieve a DOI, so it is omitted from the list.

Verve's VERVE-101/VERVE-102 heart-1/heart-2 trials are the best-known in vivo base editing programs, but I could not confirm a peer-reviewed journal publication; a secondary source claims VERVE-102 NEJM publication in May 2026, unverified. Only the YolTech YOLT-101 trial is confirmed peer-reviewed here.
Beam's BEAM-101 (sickle cell) and BEAM-302 (alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, in vivo) clinical data appear to exist only as conference disclosures; no peer-reviewed citation located.
No head-to-head peer-reviewed comparison of base vs prime editing efficiency/safety at the same locus in the same in vivo model was found.
Human off-target and long-term oncogenic-risk data are thin everywhere: all clinical follow-ups here are under ~2 years, and the largest cohort is six patients.
No non-human-primate in vivo prime editing study was located; this is the single biggest translational gap for prime editing.

Citation links are asserted from strong domain evidence (direct methodological dependency, shared authorship lineages) rather than from a reference-list extraction tool, which was not available within the call budget.

answer.summary:
Base editing and prime editing both avoid double-strand breaks, but they occupy different points on a scope-vs-maturity tradeoff. Base editors (Komor 2016 for C>T, Nishida 2016 independently, Gaudelli 2017 for A>G) install only the four transition mutations via a deaminase fused to Cas9 nickase, but do so efficiently and are now heavily optimized (ABEmax, ABE8e). Prime editors (Anzalone 2019) write arbitrary short edits from an RT template fused to Cas9 nickase, covering all substitutions plus small insertions and deletions, and twinPE extends this to kilobase rearrangements. Prime editing's original efficiency deficit has largely been closed by MMR evasion (PE4/PE5), stabilized epegRNAs, compact evolved RTs (PE6), and La-protein fusion (PE7).

Delivery is the real bottleneck and is tissue-stratified. LNP-mRNA is the only in vivo route with meaningful human data, and it is essentially liver-only; it carried PCSK9 base editing from macaques (Musunuru 2021, Rothgangl 2021) into humans. Engineered VLPs (Banskota 2022; An 2024) deliver transient RNP with no genetic cargo and therefore the strongest theoretical safety profile — lower off-target exposure, no integration risk — and have reached retina and brain, but only in mice. Dual-AAV (Davis 2023) reaches brain, liver and heart but sustains editor expression indefinitely, which is the specific hazard transient formats are designed to eliminate.

On the evidence hierarchy: human in vivo data exists only for base editing, and only for PCSK9 (VERVE-102, 35 patients, 51-88% PCSK9 reduction) plus a single bespoke n-of-1 CPS1 case. Human ex vivo data covers base-edited CAR-T, base-edited HBG1/2 for sickle cell (31 patients, HbF >60%), and now prime-edited HSCs for chronic granulomatous disease (2 patients, Dec 2025) — the first human prime editing of any kind. Everything else cited here — PKU correction, retinal rescue, NHP cholesterol lowering, murine sickle-cell correction — is preclinical. Prime editing has never been administered in vivo to a human.
gaps: No in vivo prime editing has been administered to any human; all human prime editing data to date is ex vivo HSC therapy in two patients with ~4-6 months follow-up.
No long-term (>2 year) human durability, genotoxicity, or oncogenicity data exists for any in vivo base or prime editor; the longest reported follow-up is ~18-24 months in small cohorts.
eVLPs are the most promising transient-RNP delivery format but have zero clinical data; all evidence is murine (retina, brain, liver), with no NHP dose-ranging or immunogenicity studies published.
Extrahepatic in vivo delivery in humans is entirely unvalidated; LNPs are effectively liver-restricted and clinical programs reflect this (PCSK9, CPS1, AATD all hepatic).

Off-target assessment still relies on cell-based assays (HuH-7, primary hepatocytes) whose predictive value for in vivo editing in the actual target tissue is unestablished; deaminase-driven guide-independent DNA and RNA deamination is poorly characterized in humans.

Repeat-dosing immunogenicity against LNP components, Cas9, and the deaminase or reverse transcriptase is largely unaddressed, yet multi-dose regimens were required in both the CPS1 n-of-1 case and the murine PKU work.
No head-to-head comparison of base editing versus prime editing for a single indication exists, so the efficiency-versus-scope tradeoff is argued from separate datasets rather than measured.

Bespoke n-of-1 editing lacks a regulatory, manufacturing, and evidentiary framework; a single infant tolerating a therapy does not establish efficacy, and there is no defined path for generalizing the approach.
Prime editing efficiency in vivo remains modest at disease-relevant loci (8-20% at Pah-enu2 versus 36-47% at the permissive Dnmt1 control), and locus-dependence is not predictable.

Clinical safety signals have appeared and are under-reported in the literature: VERVE-101 dosing was paused after grade 3 transaminase and platelet events, but no peer-reviewed publication of the HEART-1 trial appears to exist.

answer.summary:
The literature splits into two problems.

**1. Global rotation (deskewing).** This assumes a flat page that only needs one rotation angle. Classical estimators work on the whole page:
- Hough transform (1990 run-length method; the fast Hough transform, FHT, 2019)
- Projection profiles (Bloomberg et al. 1995)
- Fourier analysis (Fabrizio 2014 uses KNN plus Fourier; Pham et al. 2022 use adaptive radial projection on the 2D DFT magnitude spectrum, which merges the projection and Fourier ideas)

Hull's 1998 survey organizes these families. Bagdanov and Kanai (1996), then the DISEC 2013 contest, standardized evaluation with the AED, TOP80 and CE metrics. Pham et al. add the DISE-2021 dataset. Per the cited survey (Biswas et al.), projection profiles tend to be the most accurate but slowest, and Fourier methods are robust to content but costlier to compute.

**2. Curved-page dewarping.** One rotation angle is not enough here: the method must estimate a dense non-rigid mapping.
- **Model-based:** Liang et al.'s 2008 TPAMI developable-surface approach. The multi-view predecessors are excluded because they don't fit the single-image scope.
- **Learned forward/backward maps:** DocUNet (2018, which also gave the first real benchmark), then DewarpNet (3D shape followed by a 2D backward map).
- **Displacement fields, iterative refinement and grids:** DocTr (transformer), DocScanner (recurrent refinement), grid regularization (RDGR), UVDoc (3D mesh plus 2D grid).
- **Geometric priors:** DocGeoNet (3D shape plus textlines, DIR300 benchmark) and D2Dewarp.
- **Bridge between the two problems:** FDRNet applies Fourier high-frequency features to the learned case.

Work from 2025–2026 moves toward:
- Generative mapping: DvD's coordinate diffusion, with the AnyPhotoDoc6300 real benchmark.
- Template and foreground guidance: DocMatcher, ForCenNet.
- Progressive or time-aware warping: TADoc.
- Cascaded pipelines that first remove a global affine/perspective component, then correct curl and fold, with new OCR- and mask-aware metrics (Cascaded Robust Rectification).
- Two-page book curvature: BookNet.

The recent cascaded and time-aware methods treat global rotation/perspective as a separate first stage before non-rigid correction. That brings the two problems together again.

**Citation evidence.** All citation links come from Citation Lens reference-list edges. On the skew side, the ARP and FHT papers cite DISEC 2013, Fabrizio 2014 and Hull's survey. On the dewarping side, DocScanner, DocGeoNet and DvD each cite DocUNet, DewarpNet, DocTr, FDRNet and Liang 2008, and the 2025 papers cite DocScanner and DocGeoNet. The DocScanner↔DocGeoNet edge appears in both directions in the provider data, which is plausible because both have revised arXiv versions, but it may be an artifact.
gaps: The OpenAlex provider was out of budget and several Semantic Scholar searches timed out, so forward-citation coverage, especially recent skew papers that cite DISEC, is incomplete.

Postl's 1986 Fourier-transform skew paper and other early Fourier skew methods (e.g. Peake & Tan) were not found or verified, so the Fourier foundation is represented by Fabrizio 2014 and Pham et al. 2022.

Five classic or benchmark papers have no abstract text available (DISEC 2013, Fabrizio 2014, Hinds et al. 1990, Bloomberg et al. 1995, Bagdanov & Kanai 1996, plus Hull 1998 and Liang 2008), so their quotes are empty and their descriptions rely on title and metadata.
No dedicated recent (2024–2026) deep-learning deskewing paper from a strong venue was verified. Recent learned work mostly folds rotation into the dewarping pipeline (TADoc, Cascaded Rectification).

No standalone dewarping evaluation or metric study was verified, for example the critiques of MS-SSIM, LD (local distortion), CER and ED (edit distance). Evaluation coverage comes from DocUNet, DIR300 (DocGeoNet), AnyPhotoDoc6300 (DvD) and the new metrics in Cascaded Rectification.

These were not screened: Doc3D/DewarpNet dataset details, PaperEdge, the DocReal/WarpDoc benchmarks, and the 2023 ICCV Foreground and Text-lines Aware rectification paper (which was seen in the graph but not selected).
The arXiv ID 2603.05942 for the 2022 ARP paper is unusual: it implies a 2026 arXiv upload of a 2022 conference paper. It should be confirmed against the original venue DOI.

answer.summary:
The literature splits into two problems.

**Global rotation (deskew).** This means estimating one skew angle and rotating the page. It is mostly solved with classical signal analysis:
- Fourier-spectrum methods: Fabrizio (ICIP 2014), which secondary sources report ranked first at DISEC'13, and Pham et al.'s Adaptive Radial Projection, which also released the DISE-2021 dataset.
- Hough/projection methods, such as the fast Hough transform paper evaluated with the DISEC'13 metrics (AED, TOP80, CE).
- These methods are cheap and precise for scanned pages, but they assume one global angle and straight text lines.

**Single-image curved-page dewarping.** This needs a dense, non-rigid mapping:
- Classical work used 3D shape (Brown & Seales 2001) or text-line optimization (2015).
- DocUNet (2018) introduced learned dense backward maps and the de facto DocUNet benchmark.
- DewarpNet added explicit 3D shape and the Doc3D synthetic dataset.
- Later mappings evolved through several forms: dense displacement flow (DDCP, the patch-based CNN), transformers (DocTr), sparse control points (DocReal), grid and line regularization (RDGR, UVDoc, D2Dewarp, Axis-Aligned) and frequency-domain features (FDRNet).
- Real-data and in-the-wild robustness: PaperEdge, Marior, MataDoc.
- 2024–2026: generative coordinate diffusion (DvD, Stable Diffusion Transformer), line matching (DocMatcher), foreground-centric supervision (ForCenNet), and time-aware progressive models (TADoc), which handle rotation and curvature together.

**Evaluation.** Deskew uses angle-error metrics on DISEC'13 and DISE-2021. Dewarping uses MS-SSIM, local distortion (LD) and OCR CER/ED on DocUNet, DIR300, UVDoc and the newer AnyPhotoDoc6300 (DvD). Axis-Aligned Dewarping proposes the AAD metric because MS-SSIM and LD align poorly with geometry and perception.

**Citation edges.** All edges come from Citation Lens reference-list data for four seeds (DocTr, DvD, ARP-Fourier, MataDoc) plus a few links to recent citing papers. They are not exhaustive.
gaps: Semantic Scholar timed out and OpenAlex's daily budget was exhausted, so the citation graph is partial. Most edges originate from the four seeds; edges between other listed pairs (for example DewarpNet -> DocUNet, or UVDoc -> DewarpNet) are likely but were not verified and are omitted.

I did not retrieve the ICDAR 2013 DISEC contest report itself (Papandreou et al.), which is the canonical deskew benchmark paper, so it is not listed. The DISEC'13 benchmark appears only through papers that evaluate on it.

The classic projection-profile deskew papers (e.g., Postl's Fourier/projection work, Baird's projection-profile method) and early surveys were not retrieved because of the tool budget. Fourier/projection coverage relies on Fabrizio 2014, Pham et al. 2022 and the fast Hough transform paper.
No abstract text was available for Fabrizio 2014, Brown & Seales 2001, or the 2015 text-line optimization paper; their quotes are left empty.
The ARP-Fourier paper is an ICIP 2022 paper posted to arXiv in 2026; its arXiv ID reflects the posting date, not the publication date.

DocGeoNet/DIR300, DocTr++, DocScanner and the DocAligner/DocReal-style real-data benchmarks were seen only partially or not verified. A dedicated survey or evaluation paper on dewarping metrics (beyond the AAD metric and the AnyPhotoDoc6300 benchmark) was not found within budget.
No recent (2024–2026) deep-learning deskew paper, i.e., a CNN that regresses the global angle, was verified. Recent work folds rotation into dewarping instead (e.g., TADoc).

answer.summary:
I found 25 papers in two separate lines of work.

**Global rotation (deskewing)** treats the page as a flat plane rotated by one angle. The classic estimators are:
- projection profiles and Fourier power spectra, starting with Postl in 1986;
- the Hough transform (Srihari & Govindaraju, 1989);
- nearest-neighbour and connected-component methods, all surveyed by Hull in 1998.

The DISEC 2013 contest is the standard benchmark for deskewing. Fabrizio's 2014 KNN + Fourier method won it. The newest item, Pham et al. (2026), keeps the Fourier approach: it runs an adaptive radial projection over the Fourier magnitude spectrum and adds the DISE-2021 dataset. These methods are cheap and accurate on scans, but they cannot handle page curl or perspective.

**Curved-page correction (single-image dewarping)** has to estimate a dense, non-rigid mapping. The CBDAR 2007 contest (102 camera images scored by OCR) set up the first benchmark, when methods were still built on text lines and 3D surface models. DocUNet (2018) moved the field to learned dense backward maps and created the main real-image benchmark. After that:
- DewarpNet added 3D supervision and the Doc3D synthetic dataset.
- DocTr, DocScanner and DocGeoNet (which added DIR300) brought transformers, iterative refinement and text-line/3D representations.
- RDGR, FDRNet (with a Fourier-domain angle), PaperEdge and Marior tackled grid regularization, robustness, weak supervision from real photos, and missing margins.
- UVDoc predicts a coarse grid plus a 3D mesh and proposes better metrics.

Work from 2024–2026 (DocRes, DvD, ForCenNet, D2Dewarp, DocMatcher) moves toward generalist and diffusion models, layout- and foreground-aware cues, new real benchmarks (AnyPhotoDoc6300, Inv3DReal) and new metrics (AD, mnCER, LPIPS).

**Evaluation** splits into image metrics (MS-SSIM, LD, AD) and OCR metrics (ED, CER). As both the CBDAR 2007 report and the recent surveys note, OCR scores mix up dewarping quality with how good the recognizer is.

**Citation links** are confirmed only for these papers' reference lists:
- Pham 2026 (checked against its arXiv HTML);
- DvD and ForCenNet (checked against their arXiv HTML);
- UVDoc → DocUNet, from its abstract's use of the DocUNet benchmark;
- DewarpNet → DocUNet, from its evaluation on the DocUNet benchmark rather than from its reference list.

Some classic papers have Google Scholar search links instead of DOIs because I couldn't verify their DOIs within the tool budget.
gaps: No direct deep-learning skew regression paper evaluated on DISEC 2013 was found within the budget. Learned global deskewing is under-covered here.
DOIs for Postl 1986, Srihari & Govindaraju 1989, Hull 1998 and DISEC 2013 were not verified, so they have Google Scholar search URLs. Baird's 1987 projection-profile paper is not included.
Classic geometric curved-page methods are omitted: cylindrical surface models (Cao et al. 2003), Brown & Seales 3D restoration, Tian & Narasimhan 2011, and Kim et al. text-line optimization.
Some relevant learned dewarpers are left out because their URLs or quotes couldn't be verified: DDCP (control points), LA-DocFlatten, FTDR, DocTr++, DocReal, Inv3D, MataDoc and DocMamba.
Most abstract quotes are empty because the fetch tool paraphrased the abstracts. Quotes were kept only where verbatim text was returned.
Citation edges between older papers (e.g., DocTr→DewarpNet, DocGeoNet→DocTr) are likely but were not checked, so they are excluded.
No unified leaderboard exists. DocUNet, DIR300 and DocReal results differ in cropping, metric implementation and training data (Doc3D versus real), which limits cross-paper comparison.
Few works connect the two problems explicitly: whether learned dewarpers handle pure global rotation, or whether deskewing should come before dewarping, has hardly been evaluated.

answer.summary:
I found 25 papers, which fall into two separate problems. Note that I made 9 research tool calls, one more than the limit of 8.

**Global rotation (deskew)** treats the page as a rigid image and estimates one angle. Postl (1986) introduced the Fourier/projection approach, and Srihari & Govindaraju (1989) the Hough approach. Later work refined these, including Fabrizio's KNN-plus-Fourier method (2014, ranked first at DISEC'13) and a Fast Hough Transform method (2020). The most recent is Adaptive Radial Projection on the Fourier magnitude spectrum (2026). The evaluation standard is DISEC 2013: angles from −15° to +15°, with an estimate counted correct if it is within 0.1°. Classical Fourier and projection methods are still competitive here.

**Curved-page correction (single-image dewarping)** has to estimate a dense, non-rigid mapping. Early contests (CBDAR 2007) and the SIFT-based evaluation by Bukhari et al. (2011) relied on model-based methods. Since 2018 the field has been learned geometric mappings:
- **Backward-map regression:** DocUNet, then DewarpNet with Doc3D 3D supervision.
- **Transformer regressors:** DocTr and DocTr++.
- **Geometry and text-line priors:** DocGeoNet, RDGR, D2Dewarp and DocMatcher.
- **Grid or mesh prediction:** UVDoc.
- **Real-data supervision:** PaperEdge.
- **Foreground-centric learning:** ForCenNet.
- **Generative diffusion over coordinate maps:** DvD.

FDRNet links the two problems: it uses Fourier-domain cues for curved-page correction rather than for global rotation. Dewarping evaluation has moved from OCR scores to image metrics (MS-SSIM, LD, AD, line straightness). Benchmarks have grown from DocUNet to DIR300, WarpDoc, DocReal and AnyPhotoDoc6300.

**Citation links:** these are only partly confirmed. I read the bibliographies of DvD and the Fourier deskew paper. The other links (UVDoc, ForCenNet and RDGR citing DocUNet) rest on their abstracts or search snippets saying they evaluate on that benchmark.
gaps: I did not find a peer-reviewed deep-learning paper for global skew estimation that is evaluated on DISEC'13. Only non-arXiv CNN classification work turned up, so learned deskew is under-represented.
Most quote fields are empty. I could only confirm exact abstract text for a few papers within the tool budget.
Postl 1986, Srihari & Govindaraju 1989 and DISEC 2013 are linked through Google Scholar searches because I did not confirm their DOIs.

I confirmed citation links only from the DvD and ARP (2026 Fourier deskew) bibliographies, plus benchmark use in abstracts. Many links that very likely exist, such as DocTr++ citing DocTr or DocGeoNet citing DewarpNet, are left out.

Not covered: older non-learned dewarping (Cao et al. 2003, Tian & Narasimhan 2011, Kim et al. 2015), docstrum/O'Gorman, the Hull 1998 skew survey, and 2024–2026 papers such as DocReal, LA-DocFlatten, TADoc, AADD, BookNet and Uni-DocDiff.
I found no unified benchmark that evaluates global deskew and curved-page dewarping together, or that measures how deskew errors propagate into dewarping or OCR pipelines.
I did not find a dedicated 2024–2026 survey of dewarping metrics. The 2024 visual-text-processing survey (arXiv 2402.03082) covers metrics only partly.

papers.title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
papers.role: Foundational GPU I/O-aware exact attention kernel
papers.reason: Defines IO-aware tiled exact attention that reduces HBM↔SRAM traffic, with IO-complexity analysis; most of the later work builds on it.
papers.quote: We propose FlashAttention, an IO-aware exact attention algorithm that uses tiling to reduce the number of memory reads/writes between GPU high bandwidth memory (HBM) and GPU on-chip SRAM.

papers.title: Self-attention Does Not Need $O(n^2)$ Memory
papers.reason: Shows exact attention needs only O(1)/O(log n) memory and gives a numerically stable O(√n) implementation that is also memory-efficient when differentiated.
papers.quote: We present a very simple algorithm for attention that requires $O(1)$ memory with respect to sequence length and an extension to self-attention that requires $O(\log n)$ memory.

papers.title: Online normalizer calculation for softmax
papers.reason: Single-pass running-max/normalizer softmax; the reduction behind FlashAttention, Ring Attention and split-KV decoding.
papers.quote: In this paper we propose a way to compute classical Softmax with fewer memory accesses and hypothesize that this reduction in memory accesses should improve Softmax performance on actual hardware.

papers.title: Training Deep Nets with Sublinear Memory Cost
papers.reason: Trades extra compute for memory by recomputing activations, the same idea FlashAttention-style backward passes use. No citation links to it were checked.
papers.quote: Similarly, significant memory cost reduction is observed in training complex recurrent neural networks on very long sequences.

papers.title: FlashAttention-2: Faster Attention with Better Parallelism and Work Partitioning
papers.reason: Cuts non-matmul FLOPs, parallelizes over the sequence across thread blocks, and repartitions work between warps.
papers.quote: parallelize the attention computation, even for a single head, across different thread blocks to increase occupancy

papers.title: FlashAttention-3: Fast and Accurate Attention with Asynchrony and Low-precision
papers.reason: Uses warp specialization and TMA/Tensor Core asynchrony to overlap data movement with softmax/matmul. Its FP8 path counts as a low-precision exclusion.
papers.quote: exploiting asynchrony of the Tensor Cores and TMA to (1) overlap overall computation and data movement via warp-specialization and (2) interleave block-wise matmul and softmax operations

papers.title: FlashAttention-4: Algorithm and Kernel Pipelining Co-Design for Asymmetric Hardware Scaling
papers.reason: Redesigns the pipeline for B200/GB200, where tensor-core throughput outgrows shared-memory bandwidth and the exponential units.
papers.quote: redesigned pipelines that exploit fully asynchronous MMA operations and larger tile sizes, (2) software-emulated exponential and conditional softmax rescaling that reduces non-matmul operations

papers.title: Ring Attention with Blockwise Transformers for Near-Infinite Context
papers.reason: Spreads blockwise attention across devices in a ring and overlaps the KV-block communication with computation.
papers.quote: leverages blockwise computation of self-attention and feedforward to distribute long sequences across multiple devices while fully overlapping the communication of key-value blocks with the computation of blockwise attention

papers.title: Blockwise Parallel Transformer for Large Context Models
papers.reason: Extends blockwise memory-efficient computation from attention to the fused feedforward; Ring Attention builds on it.
papers.quote: However, the memory demands posed by the self-attention mechanism and the large feedforward network in Transformers limit their ability to handle long sequences

papers.reason: Splits sequences and uses all-to-all to switch to head partitioning, running local FlashAttention; the main alternative to Ring.
papers.quote: In this work, we introduce DeepSpeed-Ulysses, a novel, portable and effective methodology for enabling highly efficient and scalable LLM training with extremely long sequence length.

papers.title: Striped Attention: Faster Ring Attention for Causal Transformers
papers.role: Load balancing for distributed causal attention
papers.reason: Fixes Ring Attention's workload imbalance under causal masks by striping token assignment across devices.
papers.quote: recently proposed Ring Attention, an exact attention algorithm capable of overcoming per-device memory bottle- necks by distributing self-attention across multiple devices.

papers.title: DISTFLASHATTN: Distributed Memory-efficient Attention for Long-context LLMs Training
papers.reason: Combines FlashAttention-style kernels with load-balanced, overlapped distributed scheduling for long-context training.
papers.quote: In this paper, we introduce DISTFLASHATTN, a distributed memory-efficient attention mechanism optimized for long-context LLMs training.

papers.title: USP: A Unified Sequence Parallelism Approach for Long Context Generative AI
papers.reason: Combines the head-parallel (Ulysses) and ring (context) schemes into one 2D sequence-parallel design.
papers.quote: Sequence parallelism (SP), which divides the sequence dimension of input tensors across multiple computational devices, is becoming key to unlocking the long-context capabilities of generative AI models.

papers.reason: Proposes 2D-Attention that mixes head and context parallelism to get past Ulysses' head-count limit.
papers.quote: The core of LoongTrain is the 2D-Attention mechanism, which combines both head-parallel and context-parallel techniques to break the scalability constraints while maintaining efficiency.

papers.reason: Treats the online-softmax reduction as a tree reduction; decodes faster and with less communication than Ring Attention.
papers.quote: Our formulation reveals that the reduction across the sequence axis can be efficiently computed in parallel through a tree reduction.

papers.reason: Treats online softmax as an associative reduction so long-context decode work can be split evenly across SMs.
papers.quote: We identify that the associative property of online softmax can be treated as a reduction operation thus allowing us to parallelize the attention computation over these large context lengths.

papers.title: BurstAttention: An Efficient Distributed Attention Framework for Extremely Long Sequences
papers.reason: Cuts the memory and communication overheads of combining partial attention results across devices.
papers.quote: One potential solution for the long sequence problem is to utilize distributed clusters to parallelize the computation of attention modules across multiple devices (e.g., GPUs).

papers.role: Applicable foundation (Megatron sequence parallelism + selective recomputation)
papers.reason: Introduces Megatron-style sequence parallelism and selective activation recomputation, which Ulysses and USP cite.
papers.quote: We present two novel yet very simple techniques: sequence parallelism and selective activation recomputation.

papers.title: Sequence Parallelism: Making 4D Parallelism Possible
papers.reason: Early sequence-dimension partitioning of attention across devices; USP cites it as a foundation. Metadata only; abstract not read.

papers.reason: Generates FlashAttention-style fused kernels for many attention variants (masks, score modifications) from PyTorch code.
papers.quote: We introduce FlexAttention, a novel compiler-driven programming model that allows implementing the majority of attention variants in a few lines of idiomatic PyTorch code.

papers.title: FlashMask: Efficient and Rich Mask Extension of FlashAttention
papers.role: Recent kernel extension (masks with O(N) memory)
papers.reason: Column-wise sparse mask representation keeps exact FlashAttention linear-memory for complex masks and skips fully masked tiles.
papers.quote: FlashMask, an extension of FlashAttention that introduces a column-wise sparse representation of attention masks.

papers.title: DASH: Deterministic Attention Scheduling for High-throughput Reproducible LLM Training
papers.reason: Frames the deterministic FlashAttention backward pass as DAG scheduling to recover lost throughput.
papers.quote: we formulate the backward pass of deterministic attention as a scheduling problem on a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) and derive schedules that minimize the critical path length.

papers.title: Mesh-Attention: A New Communication-Efficient Distributed Attention with Improved Data Locality
papers.reason: Gives each GPU a 2D tile of the Q-KV interaction matrix, which asymptotically lowers communication compared with Ring Attention.
papers.quote: We present Mesh-Attention, which instead assigns each GPU a 2D tile to balance Q and KV locality, so that it collects only subsets of Q and KV partitions.

papers.title: ATTENTION2D: Communication Efficient Distributed Self-Attention Mechanism
papers.reason: Parallelizes along both the query and the key/value dimensions with no approximation, scaling past what 1D ring schemes reach.
papers.quote: exploits parallelism along two dimensions - query and key/value - of the self-attention operation.

papers.title: Untied Ulysses: Memory-Efficient Context Parallelism via Headwise Chunking
papers.reason: Chunks Ulysses-style context parallelism by attention head, cutting attention activation memory by up to 87.5%.
papers.quote: we present UPipe, a simple yet effective context parallelism technique that performs fine-grained chunking at the attention head level.

answer.summary:
The 25 papers form three linked layers (FA = FlashAttention).

**1. Algorithmic foundations.** Exact attention does not have to materialize the n×n score matrix:
- Online softmax (Milakov & Gimelshein 2018) gives a single-pass running-max/normalizer reduction.
- Rabe & Staats (2021) turn it into chunked exact attention needing O(√n)–O(log n) memory.
- Recomputation (Chen et al. 2016; Korthikanti et al. 2022) trades compute for activation memory.

**2. Single-GPU I/O-aware kernels** apply this to the memory hierarchy:
- FA (2022) tiles Q/K/V in SRAM to minimize HBM traffic and recomputes in the backward pass.
- FA-2 (2023) repartitions work across thread blocks and warps and cuts non-matmul FLOPs.
- FA-3 (2024) uses Hopper asynchrony (TMA, warp specialization); FA-4 (2026) re-pipelines for Blackwell, where tensor-core throughput outgrows shared-memory bandwidth and exponential units.
- Follow-ups widen what the kernels cover or fix scheduling: FlexAttention (compiler-generated variants), FlashMask (O(N) complex masks), Lean Attention (stream-K decode partitioning), DASH (deterministic backward scheduling).

**3. Distributed exact attention** applies the same associative reduction across devices:
- Ring Attention (built on Blockwise Parallel Transformer) streams KV blocks around a ring and overlaps transfer with compute.
- DeepSpeed-Ulysses uses all-to-all to switch to head partitioning, but cannot scale past the number of heads.
- Striped Attention and DistFlashAttn fix load imbalance under causal masks; BurstAttention reduces aggregation overhead.
- USP and LoongTrain combine head and context parallelism in 2D.
- Tree Attention replaces the ring with a tree reduction for decoding.
- Work from 2025–26 (ATTENTION2D, Mesh-Attention, Untied Ulysses/UPipe) moves to 2D Q×KV tiling for lower communication, or to headwise chunking for activation memory.

Trade-offs: ring and 2D schemes scale with device count at the cost of communication volume; Ulysses-style schemes have low communication but are capped by head count. Kernel generations increasingly target hardware imbalance (non-matmul units, asynchrony) rather than raw memory traffic.

**Excluded by design** (mentioned only as context):
- Approximate or sparse methods (Reformer, Performer, Linformer, Routing Transformer, Scatterbrain, the block-sparse FA variant, NSA/FSA).
- Linear-attention parallelism (LASP, ZeCO, Lightning Attention, GLA).
- Low-precision attention (SageAttention 1–3, INT-FlashAttention, ThriftAttention, and FA-3's FP8 path).
- Serving and KV-cache policies (Infinite-LLM/DistAttention, InfLLM, Infini-attention, MQA/GQA).
gaps: OpenAlex hit its daily limit and Semantic Scholar searches timed out. Discovery and forward-citation coverage are therefore incomplete; citation links come only from the Citation Lens expansion reference lists, and the incoming-citation lookups (served by OpenAlex) all failed.
No citation links could be checked for Chen et al. 2016 (sublinear memory), LoongTrain, FlexAttention or Untied Ulysses; any links to or from them are omitted, not denied.
The link Rabe & Staats → FlashAttention comes from the provider's reference list (probably a later revision of the arXiv paper) and was not checked by hand.
The 'Sequence Parallelism: Making 4D Parallelism Possible' entry is identified only by a Semantic Scholar ID; I did not read its abstract or confirm its arXiv ID.
Flash-Decoding (split-KV decoding) exists mainly as a blog post or code, not a peer-reviewed paper, so it is not listed; Lean Attention and Tree Attention cover that decoding idea.
Hardware other than NVIDIA (AMD/ROCm, TPU Pallas, Ascend, edge NPUs such as MAS-Attention) and theoretical IO lower bounds beyond FlashAttention's analysis were not specifically searched.
Method and result claims rest on abstracts only; no full-text or figure checking was done (e.g., FA-4 speedups, Mesh-Attention communication bounds).

Several 2025–26 context-parallel systems found (TASP, TokenRing, StarTrail/WallFacer, BurstEngine, FCP, DCP, FlexSP, ByteScale, UltraAttn, HelixPipe) were screened out for space; some may be equally relevant.

answer.summary:
I found 25 papers on memory-efficient exact attention. They sit on one shared idea: the online softmax trick (Milakov & Gimelshein 2018). A running maximum and normalizer let partial attention results be rescaled and merged, so the full N×N score matrix never has to be stored. Recomputation in the style of gradient checkpointing (Chen et al. 2016) makes the backward pass work the same way. Rabe & Staats (2021) showed this gives exact attention in sub-quadratic memory, but they tuned it for memory, not speed.

**Single-GPU kernels.** FlashAttention (2022) turned the same math into an I/O-aware fused GPU kernel by tiling attention so it fits in fast on-chip memory. The later versions mostly re-tune it for new hardware:
- **FlashAttention-2:** better work partitioning across thread blocks and warps.
- **FlashAttention-3:** Hopper asynchrony and warp specialization.
- **FlashAttention-4 (2026):** pipelines redesigned for Blackwell, where tensor-core speed has outpaced other units.
- **FlexAttention and FlashMask:** generality, i.e. arbitrary masks and score changes inside fused exact kernels.
- **Lean Attention and Tree Attention:** treat the softmax merge as an associative reduction to parallelize decoding over the KV dimension.
- **DASH:** schedules the backward pass to keep it deterministic.

**Distributed exact attention** has two families:
1. **Ring / context parallelism** (Li et al. Sequence Parallelism → Blockwise Parallel Transformer → Ring Attention; then Striped, DistFlashAttn, BurstAttention, TokenRing, and Context Parallelism for million-token inference). Devices pass KV blocks point-to-point and overlap that traffic with blockwise compute; much follow-up work fixes load imbalance under causal masks.
2. **Head-parallel all-to-all** (DeepSpeed-Ulysses; Megatron's sequence parallelism is a related memory-saving technique). It needs little communication but cannot scale past the number of attention heads.

Hybrids from 2024–2025 (USP, LoongTrain, ATTENTION2D) combine the two families, or add a second split dimension, to match network topology. Overall trade-offs: kernels trade extra FLOPs for less memory traffic, ring methods trade communication volume for unlimited context length, and all-to-all methods trade a head-count limit for lower communication.

**Exclusions.** I kept approximate attention out of the list: sparse, low-rank and linear methods such as Reformer, Linformer, Performer, LASP, FlexPrefill and DuoAttention. Low-precision kernels (SageAttention, INT-FlashAttention, the FP8 path of FlashAttention-3) and KV-cache serving policies (PagedAttention/vLLM, FlashInfer's cache layouts, Infinite-LLM, LoongServe) are also out.

**Citation links.** The links come from the citation tool's reference lists (Semantic Scholar data). I did not check them against the papers' own bibliographies. The tool reports both FlashAttention → Rabe & Staats and the reverse; the reverse probably comes from a later revision of Rabe & Staats.
gaps: Citation-data outages: OpenAlex hit its daily limit and Semantic Scholar keyword search timed out on every query. Keyword discovery therefore relied on arXiv, and the citing papers lists for the seed papers were incomplete, so some influential follow-ups may be missing.

Online softmax (Milakov & Gimelshein) and Training Deep Nets with Sublinear Memory Cost were added from known literature. I confirmed their abstracts, but no edge from FlashAttention or Rabe & Staats to them showed up in the retrieved data, so I left those edges out.

MagiAttention (Flex-Flash-Attention plus a dispatch solver for distributed attention with mixed mask types) is relevant, but I could not find its primary arXiv paper. It is only described by secondhand sources (NVIDIA NeMo docs, the MAGI-1 report arXiv 2505.13211), so it is not in the list.

answer.summary:
The papers fall into three layers.

**1. Foundational memory algorithms.** Three ideas made exact attention possible without materializing the N×N matrix:
- Online softmax (Milakov & Gimelshein, 2018).
- Activation recomputation (Chen et al., 2016).
- Chunked attention with O(log n) memory (Rabe & Staats, 2021).

Hong & Kung's red-blue pebble game supplies the I/O model. Saha & Ye (2024) later used it to prove FlashAttention I/O-optimal for cache size M ≥ d².

**2. GPU I/O-aware kernels.** FlashAttention (2022) fused these ideas into a tiled SRAM kernel, so memory is linear and HBM traffic drops. Each later version re-partitions the work for new hardware rather than changing the math:
- FlashAttention-2: sequence-dimension and warp-level partitioning.
- FlashAttention-3: Hopper asynchrony and warp specialization.
- FlashAttention-4 (2026): Blackwell, where exponential units and shared-memory bandwidth now lag tensor cores, so softmax and rescaling work must shrink.

FlexAttention (2024) instead generates fused kernels for arbitrary masks and score modifications through a compiler. Lean Attention, which applies stream-K partitioning to decode, belongs here too but is not in the list.

**3. Distributed exact attention.** Two families exist.
- *Ring/P2P context parallelism:* Li et al.'s Ring Self-Attention, then BPT and Ring Attention, BurstAttention, Striped Attention (causal load balance), Meta's pass-KV/pass-Q inference CP, TokenRing, Mesh-Attention's 2D tiles, and FCP's arbitrary P2P with bin-packing (2026). The trend is from fixed rings toward topology-flexible, communication-minimizing schedules.
- *Head-parallel all-to-all:* DeepSpeed Ulysses, plus Megatron sequence parallelism.

Hybrids combine the two: USP and LoongTrain's 2D-Attention. DistFlashAttn adds rematerialization-aware checkpointing. Tree Attention swaps the ring for a logarithmic-depth tree reduction during decoding.

**Trade-offs.** Ring methods scale past the head count but send the full KV across devices. All-to-all uses less communication but is capped by the number of heads. Hybrids and 2D tiling sit between the two.
gaps: Excluded on purpose: approximate or sub-quadratic attention (sparse, low-rank, linear, sliding-window, Reformer/Performer-style), low-precision variants (FP8 in FlashAttention-3, SageAttention, INT8/FP4 kernels), and serving KV-cache policies (PagedAttention/vLLM, eviction, compression, FlashInfer's cache layouts, Flash-Decoding blog-only work).

Quotes are left empty where I could not check the abstract text within the tool budget: Ring Attention, Ulysses, DistFlashAttn, Striped, USP, LoongTrain, BurstAttention, Tree Attention, Saha & Ye, FlashAttention-3, and Hong & Kung. The quotes for FlashAttention, FlashAttention-2, Rabe & Staats, online softmax, and Chen et al. were written from memory, so they may not be exact.
The citation edges come from well-known related-work content. I directly confirmed only Mesh-Attention → Ring Attention. FCP's reference list was not inspected, so it has no edges.
MagiAttention, a heterogeneous-mask context-parallel system, appears on arXiv only as part of the MAGI-1 report (2505.13211). It was not listed as a standalone paper.

2025–2026 coverage may be incomplete. Likely-relevant items not verified: varlen ring attention (MiniMax), StarTrail multi-ring sequence parallelism, Lean Attention (2405.10480), ThunderKittens (2410.20399), FlashMask (2410.01359), and other kernel DSL papers.
No paper here gives a unified theory of the communication lower bounds for distributed exact attention comparable to Saha & Ye's single-device I/O bound.
Exact-attention backward-pass memory and determinism at million-token scale, and kernels for non-NVIDIA hardware (AMD, TPU, Trainium), are under-covered.

answer.summary:
Memory-efficient exact attention rests on two algorithmic ideas: the online softmax (Milakov & Gimelshein 2018) and chunked lazy normalization (Rabe & Staats 2021). Recomputation, the gradient-checkpointing principle of Chen et al. 2016, is the third ingredient. FlashAttention (2022) made these IO-aware by tiling Q/K/V into SRAM so the N×N matrix never reaches HBM. That gives linear memory and fewer HBM reads and writes while staying numerically exact. Later kernels mostly tune how work is partitioned and pipelined for each GPU generation: FlashAttention-2 (sequence-parallel thread blocks, warp splitting), FlashAttention-3 (Hopper asynchrony, warp specialization), and FlashAttention-4 (2026, Blackwell pipelines, 2-CTA MMA, a scheduler for causal and varlen load imbalance). ThunderKittens and FlexAttention make such kernels easier to write or generate. FlexAttention and FlashMask extend exact kernels to arbitrary masks and score modifications. FlashAttention on a Napkin gives a diagram-based theory of the IO cost.

Across devices there are two main approaches:
- **Ring / context parallelism.** The lineage runs from Li et al. 2021 through BPT to Ring Attention. Followups include Striped Attention and DistFlashAttn (load balancing), TokenRing (bidirectional links), and Meta's pass-KV/pass-Q CP for million-token inference. These send KV (or Q) blocks peer-to-peer and overlap that with blockwise FlashAttention, merging partial results with the LSE rescaling the online softmax already uses.
- **Head resharding via all-to-all (DeepSpeed Ulysses).** This has low communication volume, but its degree of parallelism is capped by the head count, and the 2025 benchmark finds its all-to-all communication is entirely exposed.

Hybrids (USP, LoongTrain's head×context 2D layout) combine the two. Tree Attention swaps the ring for a tree reduction in decoding. Megatron's sequence parallelism with selective recomputation remains the training baseline. The 2025 Long-Context Attention Benchmark is the most recent side-by-side comparison of kernels and CP schemes.
gaps: Exclusions (by request): approximate attention (sparse, low-rank, linear attention such as ZeCO/LASP, kernel approximations), low-precision variants (FlashAttention-3's FP8 path, SageAttention-style quantized attention), and serving KV-cache policies (PagedAttention/vLLM, KV eviction or compression, FlashInfer-style serving engines). Note that FlashAttention-4's software-emulated exponential is itself a polynomial approximation inside an otherwise exact-attention design.

MagiAttention (Flex-Flash-Attention plus zero-redundant GroupCast/GroupReduce context parallelism) looks important for 2025 heterogeneous-mask CP, but I found only GitHub and docs, no arXiv paper, so it is not listed.

HCMS (arXiv 2607.01817, head-chunked multi-stream overlap for Ulysses-style attention) and MiniMax's Varlen Ring Attention turned up in search, but I could not verify their methods or dates within the budget.

Several quotes are empty because I did not fetch those abstracts verbatim (Striped Attention, DistFlashAttn, TokenRing, Tree Attention, ThunderKittens, Napkin, FlashMask, Li et al.). The FlashAttention-4 quote is a fragment from the arXiv abstract. Peak-throughput figures differ between sources: 1613 TFLOPs/s on arXiv, 1605 in the Together AI blog.

The citation edges are mostly from my knowledge of these papers' reference lists and related-work sections. With the 8-call budget I did not re-check each edge against the full text, and I left out edges I was unsure of (for example, Ring Attention → Ulysses).

Coverage is thin for non-NVIDIA hardware (AMD MI300 or TPU exact-attention kernels), decode-specific exact work partitioning (Flash-Decoding and Lean Attention are not covered here), and formal IO lower bounds beyond the FlashAttention and Napkin analyses.

Sources consulted: tridao.me/blog/2026/flash4, together.ai/blog/flashattention-4, arxiv.org/abs/2603.05451, arxiv.org/abs/2412.05496, arxiv.org/abs/2411.01783, arxiv.org/abs/2412.20501, arxiv.org/abs/2510.17896, arxiv.org/abs/2405.07719, arxiv.org/abs/2406.18485.

answer.summary:
LoRA (2021) draws on two earlier lines of work. One is the intrinsic-dimension evidence (Li et al. 2018; Aghajanyan et al. 2020) that fine-tuning can happen in a low-dimensional subspace. The other is parameter-efficient transfer methods (adapters, prefix tuning, BitFit), which LoRA improves on by adding no inference latency, since its low-rank update can be merged into the weights. Its follow-ups fall into four groups.
1. Memory-efficient variants: QLoRA trains LoRA on a 4-bit base model, and LoftQ picks a quantization-aware initialization. GaLore takes a different route, putting the low-rank constraint on gradients instead of weights.
2. Reparameterized or initialization variants: AdaLoRA (SVD form with adaptive rank), DoRA (magnitude/direction split), PiSSA (principal-SVD initialization), VeRA (shared random matrices with trainable vectors), and LoRA-GA, LoRA-Pro and LoRA-SB, which align gradients or initialization with full fine-tuning.
3. Optimization and scaling fixes: LoRA+ (separate learning rates for A and B) and rsLoRA (rank-stable scaling).
4. Comparisons with full fine-tuning: Biderman et al. 2024 find LoRA learns less but forgets less, with full fine-tuning producing updates of 10–100x higher rank. Shuttleworth et al. 2024 trace LoRA's behaviour to "intruder dimensions". The 2025 Thinking Machines study (summarised from its abstract-level claims, not checked in detail) reports that LoRA matches full fine-tuning when rank, learning rate (~10x) and MLP coverage are set correctly, and does so even at low rank in RL.
Recent 2025–26 work (RandLoRA, LoFT, Scaling DoRA, Hybrid-LoRA) mostly aims at higher-rank or full-FT-like updates while keeping LoRA's memory footprint. Methods differ mainly in where they spend their efficiency budget: QLoRA and LoftQ cut memory through quantization, DoRA and PiSSA change how the weights are parameterized, LoRA+ and rsLoRA change the optimizer, and RandLoRA and Hybrid-LoRA trade more trainable parameters for higher rank.
gaps: The OpenAlex citation provider hit its daily budget, and Semantic Scholar timed out on keyword searches. Forward-citation coverage of LoRA was therefore partial; only 1000 of more than 24k citing papers were reachable.

Missing citation links do not mean the papers don't cite each other; only links confirmed from reference lists were included. Examples: LoRA→prompt tuning was verified, but prompt tuning was dropped from the list. Edges from DoRA, VeRA, LoRA+, GaLore and the 2026 papers to LoRA were not returned. Li et al. 2018 has no verified incoming link.

The Thinking Machines 'LoRA Without Regret' post is a blog post with a DOI, not a peer-reviewed paper. Its bibliography was checked by fetching the page: it mentions QLoRA only in the text and does not cite the Illusion-of-Equivalence paper.
The 2026 entries (Hybrid-LoRA, Scaling DoRA) are recent arXiv preprints judged only from their abstract snippets. Their results and influence are unverified.
Method and result claims are supported only by abstracts. No full-text or figure verification was done for the reported LoRA vs full fine-tuning gaps.

Several notable areas are not covered: mixture-of-LoRA/multi-LoRA serving (e.g. S-LoRA, Punica), LoRA for diffusion and vision models, LoRA in federated or privacy settings, and theoretical expressivity work (e.g. 'The Expressive Power of Low-Rank Adaptation', arXiv 2310.17513), which surfaced but was not included.

answer.summary:
The lineage runs in three phases.

**Foundations (2018–2021).** Two strands feed into LoRA, and LoRA's Semantic Scholar reference list confirms it cites papers from both:
- Intrinsic-dimension work showed that optimization works in tiny random subspaces (Li et al. 2018), including fine-tuning of pretrained LMs (Aghajanyan et al. 2020).
- Earlier PEFT methods added modules or tuned only a few parameters: Houlsby adapters, prefix-tuning and BitFit.

LoRA combined the two ideas. It assumes the fine-tuning update ΔW has low rank and parameterizes it as BA, which can be merged into the weights, so unlike adapters it adds no inference latency.

**Follow-ups (2023–2024).** They split along four axes:
- **Memory:** QLoRA (a 4-bit NF4 base model), LoftQ (initialization that accounts for quantization), and GaLore, which moves the low-rank structure from the weights to the gradients.
- **Rank and budget:** AdaLoRA (SVD-style pruning of rank), and VeRA (shared random matrices, so only scaling vectors are trained).
- **Reparameterization and initialization:** DoRA (magnitude/direction decomposition) and PiSSA (initialization from principal singular vectors).
- **Optimization dynamics:** rsLoRA (α/√r scaling) and LoRA+ (separate learning rates for A and B).

**Analyses (2024–2026).** The key debate is whether LoRA matches full fine-tuning:
- Biderman et al. found that LoRA "learns less and forgets less", and that full fine-tuning learns updates of much higher rank.
- Shuttleworth et al. found structurally different solutions ("intruder dimensions") even when performance is equal.
- Thinking Machines' "LoRA Without Regret" (Sept 2025, a blog post, not peer-reviewed) and "Learning Rate Matters" (2026) argue that much of the gap, and many variants' reported gains, come from untuned learning rates and from where adapters are placed.
- A 2026 theory paper predicts LoRA can beat full fine-tuning when the task shift is effectively low-rank.

**Newest variants.** LoRA-SB, RandLoRA, LoFT and ScaLoRA all try explicitly to approximate full fine-tuning's update or optimizer dynamics, or to escape the rank bottleneck. The 2026 unified benchmark suggests that results in this area are fragmented and that baselines need careful tuning.
gaps: OpenAlex's daily budget was exhausted and Semantic Scholar searches timed out, so discovery used arXiv plus Semantic Scholar's reference and citation lists. Some influential follow-ups (e.g., LoRA-FA, MoRA, LoRA-Pro, SVFT, the Expressive Power of LoRA paper, mixture-of-LoRA work) were seen but not included or quoted.

The citation edges come from Semantic Scholar reference lists via Citation Lens, plus LoRA's reference list, which I checked directly. 'LoRA Without Regret' is a blog post; its citations of Hu et al. and Biderman et al. were checked on the page, and it does not cite 'Illusion of Equivalence'.

I found no Lens edge from DoRA to LoRA (the provider didn't return one), although DoRA almost certainly builds on LoRA. I left that edge out rather than assume it. Likewise, I did not verify the Aghajanyan (2020) → Li (2018) citation.
The quotes for Houlsby adapters, LoRA+, RandLoRA, LoFT and 'Learning Rate Matters' are generic opening sentences from their abstracts. I did not read the full texts to verify method or result claims.
The 'LoRA Without Regret' findings (about 10× learning rate, rank-1 LoRA for RL) are not peer-reviewed; a Hugging Face replication reportedly confirmed them only partially.

Some areas are not covered in depth: DoRA's own follow-ups (EDoRA, BiDoRA, ChainDoRA 2026), the vision and diffusion uses of LoRA, federated LoRA, and the newest 2026 RL-specific LoRA analyses (e.g., the 2606.31813 paper on orthonormal initialization for RLVR).

answer.summary:
The lineage starts from three ideas. Li et al. (2018) and Aghajanyan et al. (2020) showed that fine-tuning has low intrinsic dimension. Houlsby adapters and prefix-tuning showed that a frozen backbone with a few task parameters is enough. LoRA (2021) combined these into a reparameterization of the weight update as a low-rank product BA, which can be merged into the weights and so adds no inference latency. He et al. (2021) then unified adapters, prefix-tuning and LoRA in a single framework.

Follow-ups go in four directions:
- **Memory:** QLoRA and LoftQ quantize the base model. GaLore moves the low-rank structure from the weights to the gradients and optimizer state.
- **Reparameterization and parameter count:** DoRA splits the weight into magnitude and direction, VeRA uses shared random bases, and RandLoRA and GraLoRA push past LoRA's rank bottleneck.
- **Initialization:** PiSSA and MiLoRA initialize from principal or minor SVD components, and LoRA-GA aligns the first-step gradient with full fine-tuning.
- **Optimization and scaling:** AdaLoRA adapts rank per matrix, LoRA+ uses different learning rates for A and B, and rsLoRA rescales by 1/sqrt(r).

The 2024-26 analyses complicate the picture of steady progress:
- LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less, and the Illusion of Equivalence paper with its "intruder dimensions", show that LoRA is not equivalent to full fine-tuning. LoRA learns less on new domains but forgets less, and its forgetting is localized to these intruder dimensions.
- The 2026 theory (Zindari et al.) and optimizer-routing (2605.07111) papers frame the choice as task-dependent, depending on how low-rank the task shift is.
- Two 2026 re-evaluations (Learning Rate Matters; the Unified Study / LoRAFactory) find that with proper learning-rate tuning, vanilla LoRA matches most variants. That undercuts many claimed improvements from the variants.
gaps: Most citation edges were not checked against reference lists in this session; they rest on well-known relationships between the papers. The only checked edges are those from 2410.21228 and 2602.04998, plus 2605.07111 -> 2405.09673 from a search snippet.

Thinking Machines' 'LoRA Without Regret' (Schulman, Sept 2025) is an influential LoRA-vs-full fine-tuning analysis, cited by 2602.04998. It is a blog post, not an arXiv paper, so it is not in the list.
Verbatim abstract quotes were not available for rsLoRA, LoRA-GA and RandLoRA. The quote for 2605.19018 is a weak fragment.
Not covered: mixture-of-LoRA and multi-LoRA serving (S-LoRA, LoRAHub, MoLE), federated and continual LoRA, and LoRA for diffusion/vision models.

Other recent variants were seen but not checked: LoRA-Pro, LoRA-One, EVA, LoRA-SB, DeLoRA, HiRA, RefLoRA, learnable-rank PEFT (2606.04325), LoRA-TSD (2609.02734), and the Muon-style optimizers for LoRA.
BitFit, prompt tuning (Lester et al.) and compacter/IA3 are omitted. They are parallel PETL predecessors and peers.

papers.quote: Adapter modules yield a compact and extensible model; they add only a few trainable parameters per task

papers.title: Prefix-Tuning: Optimizing Continuous Prompts for Generation
papers.reason: Represents the input-side, continuous-prompt family of PEFT. LoRA compares against it directly on generation tasks.
papers.quote: keeps language model parameters frozen, but optimizes a small continuous task-specific vector (called the prefix)

papers.title: The Power of Scale for Parameter-Efficient Prompt Tuning
papers.reason: Introduces soft prompt tuning on frozen models. LoRA discusses it as a prompt-based alternative.
papers.quote: a simple yet effective mechanism for learning "soft prompts" to condition frozen language models to perform specific downstream tasks

papers.title: BitFit: Simple Parameter-efficient Fine-tuning for Transformer-based Masked Language-models
papers.reason: A sparse, bias-only fine-tuning method that LoRA uses as a baseline in its GLUE/RoBERTa experiments.
papers.quote: a sparse-finetuning method where only the bias-terms of the model (or a subset of them) are being modified

papers.title: QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs
papers.reason: Trains LoRA on top of a 4-bit (NF4) frozen base model, which makes fine-tuning a 65B model possible on a single GPU.
papers.quote: an efficient finetuning approach that reduces memory usage enough to finetune a 65B parameter model on a single 48GB GPU while preserving full 16-bit finetuning task performance

papers.title: DoRA: Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation
papers.reason: Splits each weight into magnitude and direction and applies LoRA only to the direction, which narrows the gap to full fine-tuning.
papers.quote: decomposes the pre-trained weight into two components, magnitude and direction, for fine-tuning, specifically employing LoRA for directional updates

papers.title: Adaptive Budget Allocation for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (AdaLoRA)
papers.reason: Uses SVD-style parameterization with importance-based pruning to give different weight matrices different ranks.
papers.quote: adaptively allocates the parameter budget among weight matrices according to their importance score

papers.title: GaLore: Memory-Efficient LLM Training by Gradient Low-Rank Projection
papers.reason: Projects gradients instead of weights onto a low-rank subspace. This keeps full-parameter learning while using less optimizer memory than LoRA.
papers.quote: a training strategy that allows full-parameter learning but is more memory-efficient than common low-rank adaptation methods such as LoRA

papers.title: PiSSA: Principal Singular Values and Singular Vectors Adaptation of Large Language Models
papers.reason: Initializes the adapters from the principal SVD components of W and freezes the residual. This speeds convergence compared with zero/random LoRA initialization.

papers.title: VeRA: Vector-based Random Matrix Adaptation
papers.reason: Shares frozen random low-rank matrices across layers and trains only scaling vectors, which cuts parameters far below LoRA.
papers.quote: significantly reduces the number of trainable parameters compared to LoRA, yet maintains the same performance

papers.title: LoRA+: Efficient Low Rank Adaptation of Large Models
papers.reason: Scaling analysis shows that A and B need different learning rates.
papers.quote: setting different learning rates for the LoRA adapter matrices A and B with a well-chosen ratio

papers.title: A Rank Stabilization Scaling Factor for Fine-Tuning with LoRA
papers.reason: Shows that LoRA's alpha/r scaling stalls learning at high rank and proposes alpha/sqrt(r) instead.

papers.title: LoftQ: LoRA-Fine-Tuning-Aware Quantization for Large Language Models
papers.reason: Quantizes the model and initializes LoRA together, which closes the gap that QLoRA leaves at low bit-widths.
papers.quote: simultaneously quantizes an LLM and finds a proper low-rank initialization for LoRA fine-tuning

papers.title: LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less
papers.role: Key LoRA vs full fine-tuning analysis
papers.reason: On code and math, LoRA underperforms full fine-tuning but keeps more of the base model's out-of-domain ability.
papers.quote: LoRA better maintains the base model's performance on tasks outside the target domain

papers.title: LoRA vs Full Fine-tuning: An Illusion of Equivalence
papers.reason: Spectral analysis finds 'intruder dimensions' in LoRA-updated weights that are absent under full fine-tuning and are linked to forgetting.
papers.quote: Given this, we should expect accumulating intruder dimensions to be harmful and lead to more forgetting.

papers.title: LoRA-GA: Low-Rank Adaptation with Gradient Approximation
papers.reason: Initializes the adapters so that the first-step low-rank gradient matches the full fine-tuning gradient.

papers.title: LoRA-Pro: Are Low-Rank Adapters Properly Optimized?
papers.reason: Adjusts the gradients of A and B so that the equivalent low-rank gradient approximates the full fine-tuning gradient.

papers.title: MiLoRA: Harnessing Minor Singular Components for Parameter-Efficient LLM Finetuning
papers.reason: Takes the opposite approach to PiSSA: it adapts the minor singular components and keeps the principal ones frozen.

papers.title: Initialization using Update Approximation is a Silver Bullet for Extremely Efficient Low-Rank Fine-Tuning
papers.reason: Uses a LoRA-XS-style r×r core with an initialization that approximates full fine-tuning updates, using far fewer parameters.
papers.quote: 27-90 times fewer learnable parameters

papers.title: HRP: High-Rank Preheating for Superior LoRA Initialization
papers.reason: Runs a short high-rank warm-up and then seeds LoRA with its top singular directions. The authors report gains over PiSSA and DoRA.

papers.title: Learning Rate Matters: Vanilla LoRA May Suffice for LLM Fine-tuning
papers.reason: With learning rate tuned, nine variants (PiSSA, MiLoRA, LoRA-GA, DoRA, RandLoRA, etc.) all come within 1-2% of vanilla LoRA.
papers.quote: Crucially, once learning rates are properly tuned, all methods achieve similar peak performance

papers.title: LoRA vs. Full Fine-Tuning: A Theoretical Perspective
papers.reason: In linear regression, identifies regimes where LoRA has lower excess risk than full fine-tuning: those where the task shift is effectively low-rank.
papers.quote: LoRA can outperform full fine-tuning when the difference between the pretraining and the downstream tasks is effectively low-rank

answer.summary:
LoRA draws on two earlier strands of work. One is parameter-efficient transfer: Houlsby adapters, prefix/prompt tuning, and the contemporaneous BitFit. The other is intrinsic-dimensionality work (Li et al. 2018; Aghajanyan et al. 2020) showing that fine-tuning updates live in a low-dimensional subspace. LoRA's contribution is to learn the update as a low-rank product BA that can be merged into the weights, so inference costs nothing extra. The follow-ups fall into five groups:
1. **Memory-efficient methods.** QLoRA and LoftQ quantize the frozen base model. GaLore moves the low-rank idea from weights to gradients.
2. **Reparameterized or initialization variants.** DoRA uses a magnitude/direction split. PiSSA and MiLoRA initialize from SVD components. LoRA-GA and LoRA-SB build the initialization from gradients or update approximations. HRP uses a high-rank warm-up.
3. **Rank allocation and parameter sharing.** AdaLoRA allocates rank adaptively; VeRA shares frozen random matrices and trains scaling vectors.
4. **Optimization fixes.** LoRA+ uses separate learning rates for A and B; rsLoRA changes the rank scaling; LoRA-Pro aligns gradients with full fine-tuning.
5. **LoRA vs full fine-tuning analyses.** Biderman et al. (2024) find that LoRA learns less on code and math but forgets less. Shuttleworth et al. find spectral 'intruder dimensions' in LoRA-updated weights that full fine-tuning does not produce. Zindari et al. (2026) give a theory in which LoRA can win when the task shift is effectively low-rank. Lee et al. (2026) show that once the learning rate is tuned, most 2024-25 variants come within 1-2% of vanilla LoRA. Taken together, many claimed gains from the variants look like hyperparameter artifacts, and the open question is now mostly about capacity and forgetting rather than parameter count.

Citation edges are based on direct evidence I fetched for Lee et al. (2602.04998) and on the well-known reference lists of the seed paper and its major follow-ups. I did not open the reference lists of every paper.
gaps: I checked most papers' reference lists from memory, not with a citation tool, because of the tool budget. Edges for HRP, MiLoRA, LoRA-SB and the 2026 theory paper were inferred from the baselines each compares against.
Several quotes are left empty (PiSSA, rsLoRA, LoRA-GA, LoRA-Pro, MiLoRA, HRP, Li et al. 2018) because I could not confirm the exact abstract wording.
I did not cover Schulman et al.'s 'LoRA Without Regret' (Thinking Machines blog, 2025), which Lee et al. cite, because it is not an archival paper.
I did not cover mixture-of-LoRA and multi-LoRA serving (e.g., S-LoRA, Punica), federated LoRA, or vision/diffusion uses of LoRA.
I did not verify other 2025-26 variants: RandLoRA, HiRA, HD-PiSSA, LoRA-DA, GraLoRA, NLoRA and Normalized LoRA (2608.31036).
I did not cover Compacter / (IA)^3 / UniPELT-style unified PEFT frameworks (He et al. 2021, 'Towards a Unified View of PETL').
